title: Moving Students Past “I Suck as a Writer.”
author: Kelly Gallagher
summary: Kelly Gallagher takes a Harlan Coben line about bad writers as a prompt to ask how teachers move students past the belief that they are poor writers. He cites research that more than a third of second graders already think they are not good writers, and that the belief persists through high school. His answer is volume: students need lots of low-pressure, ungraded writing away from the teacher's eyes, since a great deal of bad writing must happen before good writing emerges. He teaches students that all first drafts are poor, borrows Anne Lamott's down draft, up draft and dental draft, and uses the RADaR moves of replace, add, delete and rearrange. Having students record themselves reading their essays aloud helps them hear problems silent reading misses. He closes by saying that no standard matters if students are not writing constantly, followed by an amusing postscript about being named in a Coben novel.
points: Self-doubt about writing begins early, so teachers should expect and normalize it rather than argue students out of it.
Volume of low-stakes, ungraded writing is presented as the most direct way to build fluency and confidence.
RADaR gives students four concrete revision moves, and revision should be taught from day one, before editing for correctness.
Reading drafts aloud, ideally recorded, surfaces revision needs and helps students develop a writer's voice.
quotes: A ton of bad writing has to happen before good writing emerges (to paraphrase Peter Elbow: “You have to play a lot of bad piano before you can play good piano”).
Instead, students should be producing lots of low-pressure, ungraded writing—away from the eyes of the teacher.
Becoming a better writer is first and foremost a volume issue. The best teaching of writing is the writing.
It’s also important that students understand that all first-draft writing sucks. 100% of initial drafts.
(Note: making it better is not the same thing as making it correct. The stuff needs to get better before the writer is concerned with correctness. Revision comes before editing.)
Reading aloud catches problems that silent reading misses. Oral reading also helps students develop an ear—which is how a writer’s voice begins to emerge.
You can teach every writing standard, but if students are not writing and writing and writing, it will not matter.
